lead: A part program is a list of blocks. Each block tells the machine where to go, how fast to move, and which spindle and tool to use. Manual part programming means a person writes these blocks from a drawing, without CAM software. It still matters for small shops, repairs, simple profiles and learning what the controller actually does. A clear program also prevents crashes: the safe start block, work offset, tool length and cutter radius compensation are set before the first cut. The same G-code structure runs a milling machine and a lathe, with small differences in feed units and cycles.
prereq: You need 6.3 for interpolation and work offsets, and Unit 5 for cutting speed and feed.

blocks.text: One block is one line. A word is an address letter plus a number. N numbers the block. G selects a preparatory mode. X, Y, Z are coordinates; I, J, K are arc centre offsets from the arc start; R is the arc radius when a G02/G03 arc is written with a radius instead of I and J, and the retract plane level in a canned cycle. The working plane is selected by G17 (XY), G18 (ZX) or G19 (YZ), not by R. F is feed, S spindle speed, T tool, M a switching code. Write words in the order N, G, X, Y, Z, I, J, K, F, S, T, M. Most controllers accept another order, but this order is easy to check.

A modal word stays active in later blocks until replaced. G01 remains the motion mode after it is written; a later block with only X and Y still feeds. A non-modal word acts only in its own block, such as G04 dwell or G28 return to reference.

Start every program with a safe start block: N10 G21 G90 G54 G40 G49 G80. G21 selects millimetres, G90 absolute coordinates, G54 the first work offset, G40 cancels cutter radius compensation, G49 cancels tool length compensation, G80 cancels canned cycles. This puts the machine in a known state before the first move.

G00 is rapid traverse, not a cutting move. G01 is straight-line feed. G02 and G03 are circular arcs; G02 is clockwise and G03 counter-clockwise seen looking down the +Z axis towards the work. An arc block gives the end point and the centre via I and J from the arc start.

G90 uses absolute coordinates from work zero; G91 uses increments from the current point. From X50 Y20, G90 X80 Y40 reaches X80 Y40. G91 X30 Y20 also reaches X80 Y40. G54 to G59 are work offsets that store part zero relative to machine zero.

G41 and G42 switch cutter radius compensation on, left and right of the direction of travel. Program the part outline; the controller shifts the tool centre by the cutter radius from the D register. G40 cancels. G43 applies tool length compensation from the H register, so Z is measured to the tool tip. G49 cancels.
Canned cycles compress repeated motions. G81 drills to depth and retracts. G83 peck drills in steps to clear chips. G84 taps. On a lathe, G71 roughs a profile in two blocks and G70 finishes it.
F is mm/min on a mill and mm/rev on a lathe. S is rev/min. T selects a tool. M03 and M04 start the spindle forward and reverse, M05 stops it, M06 changes tool, M30 ends the program.

Plan the process before writing blocks: choose work zero, list tools, write the safe start block, start the spindle, position clear of the work, cut, cancel compensation, retract, stop the spindle, end. For a contour, start outside a corner so G41 can build its offset before the first cut.

The worked example mills an 80 mm by 50 mm contour with a 10 mm cutter. The tool centre runs 5 mm outside, on a 90 mm by 60 mm path. At 150 mm/min the cutting time is 2.00 min. The figure shows corners A, B, C and D and the joining moves.

This turning program faces a 32 mm blank and turns a 20 mm diameter for 30 mm, then a 30 mm diameter for the next 20 mm. G97 selects direct spindle speed, here 1000 rev/min. G71 takes 1 mm depth of cut (U1.0) and leaves 0.2 mm on diameter and 0.05 mm on the face for G70.

figure.caption: The four corners A, B, C and D of an 80 mm by 50 mm contour, traced clockwise as the program does. The edge labels are the G01 moves that join them; with G41 the tool centre runs 5 mm outside this outline.

spec.aria: A directed rectangle traced clockwise: from A at X0 Y0 the move G01 Y50 goes to D at X0 Y50, then X80 goes to C at X80 Y50, then Y0 goes to B at X80 Y0, then X0 returns to A.

examples.question: A rectangular contour 80 mm by 50 mm is milled round the outside with a 10 mm diameter end mill at 150 mm/min. Write the main blocks with G41 and G54, and find the cutting time. Compare with the time without G41.
steps: With G41 the tool centre is 5 mm left of the clockwise path, outside the part. Offset rectangle: 80 + 2×5 = 90 mm; 50 + 2×5 = 60 mm.
Contour time = 300 ÷ 150 = 2.00 min. This is the contour only; the lead-in from X-10 Y-10 to X0 Y0 and the lead-out back to X-10 Y-10 are left out.
Each lead move is √(10² + 10²) ≈ 14.1 mm. Counting both, the path is 300 + 14.1 + 14.1 ≈ 328 mm and the time is 328 ÷ 150 ≈ 2.19 min.
Without G41: path = 2 × (80 + 50) = 260 mm; time = 260 ÷ 150 = 1.73 min. The part is 10 mm smaller in each dimension.
examples.answer: Cutting time with G41 is 2.00 min; without compensation it is 1.73 min, but the part is undersize by 10 mm in each dimension.
examples.check:
L=80
W=50
d=10
r=d/2
F=150
Lp=L+2*r
Wp=W+2*r
P=2*(Lp+Wp)
t=P/F
P0=2*(L+W)
t0=P0/F
print(P)
print(F)
print(f'{t:.2f}')
print(P0)
print(f'{t0:.2f}')

traps: G02 and G03 are judged looking down the +Z axis towards the work, not from the side. G02 is clockwise.
Do not mix G90 and G91 in one pass. Every coordinate after a change follows the new rule.
F is mm/min on a mill but mm/rev on a lathe. F0.2 on a lathe means 0.2 mm per revolution, the same number 0.2 on a mill would mean 0.2 mm/min.
G41 and G42 depend on travel direction. Reverse the path and the same outside contour needs the other code.
G01 is modal; a block with only X and Y still feeds, not rapid.

quiz.a: A code that stays active in later blocks until another code of the same group replaces it.
G80 cancels any active canned cycle.

quiz.q: Why is a safe start block written first?
quiz.a: It sets units, absolute mode, work offset and cancels compensation and cycles, so the machine starts from a known state and does not inherit an old mode.

quiz.q: From X40 Y10, what point does G91 X20 Y-5 reach?
quiz.a: X = 40 + 20 = 60 mm; Y = 10 − 5 = 5 mm. The point is X60 Y5.

quiz.q: A 60 mm by 40 mm contour is milled with a 12 mm cutter at 120 mm/min using G41. Find the offset path length and cutting time.
quiz.a: r = 12 ÷ 2 = 6 mm; offset rectangle 60 + 12 = 72 mm by 40 + 12 = 52 mm; path = 2 × (72 + 52) = 248 mm; time = 248 ÷ 120 = 2.07 min.

quiz.q: Why does G41 avoid an undersize part when the program follows the part outline?
quiz.a: G41 shifts the tool centre by the cutter radius away from the programmed line, so the cutting edge, not the tool centre, follows the outline. Without it the centre follows the line and the cutter removes a radius of material from the part side.

quiz.q: Explain the two blocks of a G71 turning cycle and the role of G70.
quiz.a: The first G71 block gives depth of cut and retract. The second gives the profile start and end blocks, finishing allowances and feed. G71 removes the bulk of material; G70 repeats the same profile as a finish pass.

beyond: Not for the exam. Shop-floor programmers use parametric macros, subprograms and probing cycles to make families of parts. CAM systems generate the same blocks from a model; see 6.5. Modern controllers also accept high-level cycles and conversational input. Search for Fanuc macro variables, Siemens ShopMill cycles, and ISO 6983.
